title: The Girl Who Gave Away Her Reflection
summary: Elsie dislikes her own reflection so much that she trades it away to a mirror-merchant, so she never has to see herself again. But a person without a reflection slowly forgets who she is, and Elsie must win back the face she gave away — and learn to meet her own eyes with kindness.

chapters.title: The Face She Couldn't Stand
chapters.body:
Elsie was twelve, and she could not stand the sight of her own face.

It was not that anything was wrong with it. To everyone else, Elsie looked perfectly ordinary — a pleasant, unremarkable girl's face, no better or worse than most. But Elsie, when she looked in a mirror, saw only things to dislike. Her nose was wrong. Her eyes were too far apart, or too close, she could never decide which. Her smile was crooked. Her whole face, when she looked at it, filled her with a hot uncomfortable feeling — a mix of shame and dissatisfaction and a wish to be someone else. She avoided mirrors when she could. And when she couldn't — catching her reflection in a window, a pond, a polished spoon — she flinched away, hating what she saw.

It was a miserable way to live, flinching from your own face, and Elsie was tired of it. So when a strange merchant came to the village with a cart full of mirrors — mirrors of every kind, in frames of silver and bone and dark wood — and offered a peculiar service, Elsie was ready to listen.

"I deal in reflections," the mirror-merchant said, a thin figure with a face oddly hard to look at directly. "I can take a reflection you don't want, and keep it, so you never have to see it again. Trade me your reflection, and when you look in any mirror, any pond, any polished thing — you'll see nothing. No face. No self. Never again the sight that troubles you." The merchant smiled a thin smile. "Most people cling to their reflections, of course. But now and then I meet someone who'd give anything not to have to look at themselves. And to them, I offer the trade."

Elsie should have wondered why the merchant collected reflections, and what it cost to give one away. But she was so tired of hating her own face that the offer seemed like a mercy — to never have to see herself again, to be free of the hot shameful flinching feeling forever. So she agreed. The merchant held up a dark mirror, and Elsie looked into it, and felt something pull loose from her — her reflection, drawn out of her and into the merchant's mirror, where her ordinary, disliked face now hung, trapped, staring back out at her one last time before the merchant covered it with a cloth.

And from that moment, Elsie had no reflection. She looked in the village pond, and saw only water. She looked in her mother's mirror, and saw only the room behind her, no face at all. She had given her face away, and now, when she looked for herself, she found nothing there.

And at first, it was exactly the relief she'd hoped for. No more flinching. No more hot shame. No more disliked face staring back at her. Elsie walked through her days lighter, freed from the sight of herself, and thought she'd made a wonderful trade.

But a person is not meant to have no reflection. And slowly, Elsie began to discover why.

chapters.title: The Girl Who Forgot Herself
chapters.body:
The trouble began quietly, and grew.

Without a reflection, Elsie found, she began to forget what she looked like. This seemed like no great loss at first — why should she want to remember a face she'd disliked? But it went further than she expected. As the weeks passed, and she never once saw her own face, the memory of it faded, and then blurred, and then vanished — until Elsie could not, however hard she tried, picture her own face at all. And she found, to her surprise, that this troubled her deeply. Because a person's face, it turns out, is tied to their sense of who they are. And as Elsie lost the image of her own face, she began, in a strange and frightening way, to lose her sense of herself.

It crept in slowly. She'd feel uncertain, in a way she couldn't name — unsure of who she was, unsure of her own edges, as if without a face to return to she were slowly becoming no one. When people spoke to her, she felt oddly insubstantial, like a person who wasn't quite there. She would reach for her sense of herself — the solid feeling of being Elsie, a particular person — and find it thinning, blurring, slipping away, the same way her remembered face had slipped away. Because a reflection, she was learning, is not just an image you look at. It's a kind of anchor. It's the daily meeting with yourself that reminds you that you are someone, a particular person, here, real. Take it away, and you begin to come untethered — to forget not just your face, but your self.

And there was something worse. Elsie had given her reflection away because she hated it. But she came to understand that in refusing ever to look at herself, she had not escaped the problem — she had made it permanent. Her dislike of her face had never really been about her face. It had been about how she looked at it — with shame, with harshness, with a merciless eye that found only flaws. And by giving the face away instead of learning to look at it kindly, she had frozen that harsh dislike forever, unhealed, unresolved. She had run from the mirror instead of learning to meet it, and running had not fixed the hating; it had just buried it, along with her whole sense of who she was.

Elsie went to find the mirror-merchant, frightened now, to beg for her reflection back. She found the cart of mirrors still in the village, and the thin hard-to-look-at merchant beside it, and she pleaded for the return of her face.

"Ah," the merchant said, unsurprised. "They always come back. They think giving away their reflection will free them from hating it. But a person without a reflection forgets who they are — you're fading already, I can see it, going thin and uncertain. You want your face back now." The merchant's thin smile returned. "I'll return it. I don't keep reflections against their owners' will. But understand, girl — I can give you back the face. I cannot give you back the thing you actually need, which is the ability to look at it without hating it. If I return your reflection, and you look at it the same way you always did — with shame, with harshness — you'll be right back where you started, flinching from yourself, and you'll only want to give it away again. The face was never your problem. The way you look at it was. And that, no merchant can trade for you. That, you have to learn yourself."

And Elsie understood that getting her reflection back was only half of what she needed — and that the harder half was something she would have to do on her own.

chapters.title: Meeting Her Own Eyes
chapters.body:
The mirror-merchant returned Elsie's reflection — drew it out from under the cloth and gave it back to her, so that when she next looked in a mirror, there was her face again, ordinary as ever, staring back. And with her face came back her sense of herself, the anchor restored, the fading reversed. She was Elsie again, solid and real and here. But her face was still the face she had disliked, and now she had to do the hard thing the merchant had said no one could do for her: she had to learn to look at it without hating it.

It did not come easily. The first time Elsie stood before a mirror after getting her reflection back, the old hot shameful feeling rose up at once — the merciless eye, cataloguing flaws, the nose, the eyes, the crooked smile. But now Elsie understood that this way of looking was the real problem, and that if she didn't change it, she'd be trapped forever, either flinching from her face or giving it away and losing herself. So she made herself keep looking. And instead of hunting for flaws, she tried — clumsily, at first — to look at her own face the way she might look at a friend's.

Because that was the thing she realized: she would never look at a friend's face the way she looked at her own. If a friend had her exact face, she would never think it wrong, or ugly, or shameful. She'd think it was just her friend's face — ordinary and dear and simply theirs. The cruelty was one she reserved entirely for herself. She looked at everyone else with kindness, or at least with fairness, and only at herself with this merciless, flaw-hunting eye. And that wasn't because her face was worse than everyone else's. It was just a bad habit of looking — a harshness she'd turned on herself and no one else.

So Elsie practiced looking at her own face kindly. Every day, she stood before the mirror, and when the old harsh eye rose up, she gently set it aside, and tried to see her face the way she'd see a friend's — with fairness, with warmth, with acceptance. It was hard, and it was slow, and at first it felt false. But little by little, it began to work. She'd look at her nose, and instead of wrong, she'd think, that's just my nose, it's fine, it's mine. She'd look at her crooked smile, and instead of shame, she'd feel a small fondness — it was her smile, after all, the one she smiled at people she loved. Day by day, the merciless eye softened, and the hot shameful feeling faded, and Elsie learned, slowly, to meet her own eyes in the mirror with kindness instead of cruelty.

And here was the wonderful thing she discovered: her face didn't change at all, but everything changed. It was the same ordinary face it had always been — same nose, same eyes, same crooked smile. But once she looked at it kindly, it stopped troubling her. It became, simply, her face — not a catalogue of flaws, not a source of shame, just the dear ordinary face she met each morning, hers and fine and even, on good days, rather nice. The problem had never been the face. It had been the looking. And when she healed the looking, the face was fine, exactly as it had always secretly been.

Elsie never gave her reflection away again. She kept it, and met it daily, and looked at herself with the same kindness she gave everyone else — which was all she'd ever needed to do. And she understood, now, the whole of the thing. You cannot escape a face you dislike by giving it away; you only lose yourself, because your reflection is the anchor of who you are. And you cannot fix the dislike by never looking; you only freeze it, unhealed. The only way out is the hard way, the inward way: to learn to look at yourself with kindness — to meet your own eyes the way you'd meet a friend's, with fairness and warmth and acceptance — until the face that troubled you becomes, simply, your face, dear and ordinary and fine.

And when she grew up, and met young people who flinched from their own reflections, who hated their faces and wished them away, Elsie told them what she'd learned. She told them the face was never the problem — the harsh eye they turned on themselves was. She told them you can't escape yourself by looking away, only by learning to look kindly. And she taught them to do the hardest and most freeing thing there is: to stand before the mirror, and meet their own eyes, and offer themselves the same kindness they'd offer anyone else — until, at last, they could look at their own dear ordinary faces, and not flinch, but simply, gently, see themselves, and find that it was fine. That they were fine. That they always, underneath the cruel looking, had been.
